book_context: A 1915 prologue of the Lusitania hand-off is followed by the post-war comic thriller. Tommy and Tuppence form a 'joint venture'. A chance-overheard name, Jane Finn, triggers Whittington's panic, and that leads to Carter, Julius and Mr. Brown. Recurring mechanisms include: advertisements; coincidence as a theme; bluffing about how much one knows; money and marriage talk that pays off in two proposals; the hidden master criminal who uses 'Brown' and plays nonentities. Planted details pay off later: the clerk Brown, Rita, the Paris pensionnat, the Esthonia firm, the green toque, the hospital meeting and Tommy's uncle. In early chapters the girl's identity, Danvers's name and Brown's identity must not be disclosed beyond what the text shows.
continuity_checks: Tuppence cannot understand Whittington's reaction; the narration must not explain it.
She does not yet connect the name to Tommy's overheard remark (that happens in Ch. III).
Clerk Brown is not singled out by the narrator.

essential: Tuppence's initial suspicion of the stranger's motive is dispelled. She dislikes him instinctively: a big, clean-shaven man with a heavy jowl and small, shifty eyes.
He overheard them in Lyons' and followed her. His card reads Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co. He sets an appointment for 11 tomorrow.
Her terrier-like shake of the shoulders, and her resolve.
She telegraphs Tommy at his club, using his retained pencil: 'Don't put in advertisement. Will explain to-morrow.' She weighs ninepence against five shillings.
Office: a dirty outer office with a middle-aged clerk, then a private room. Whittington is sleek and shifty.

The offer: £100 plus expenses for three months at Madame Colombier's pensionnat in Paris, as his ward, with no contact with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American, given her picked-up accent, from an American hospital pal.
She says the terms are too liberal, and he gives his justification. She insists her partner Beresford comes too: 'both or neither'.
Asked her name, she blurts 'Jane Finn' to protect her father. He reacts with purple rage and dismay, believes she has been playing him, and asks 'Rita?'
Her truthful bluffs: 'Rita knows nothing about me', 'Very little indeed', 'It might be my own name', 'by chance'. Each one increases his unease.
She plays the adventuress ('live by my wits'). Keep 'Blackmail, eh?' answered by 'payment of services in advance', and his grudging admiration.
The clerk brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington dismisses 'Brown', defers the meeting to the same time tomorrow and pays £50. His renewed geniality gives her a faint misgiving.
She takes a taxi to meet Tommy at five to twelve and makes the five-pound-note line.
optional: Dream of Esthonia Glassware as hospital plates (p28).
Walking up the street to avoid looking eager, and taking the stairs (p29–30).
Penny buns and the vicarage reflection can shrink to one clause, but keep the meagre-breakfast motive for 'how much do you want' if feasible.
The government pen 'treacle' joke (p24), while keeping Tommy's pencil.

title: MR. WHITTINGTON’S OFFER

verbatim.text: And as I’ve said before, and shall doubtless say again, little Tuppence can look after herself, thank you!”

verbatim.purpose: Whittington's wording hints at an impersonation without stating it.
verbatim.text: What I am willing to pay for is a young lady with sufficient intelligence and presence of mind to sustain her part well, and also one who will have sufficient discretion not to ask too many questions.
“Jane Finn,” she said hastily; and then paused open-mouthed at the effect of those two simple words.

verbatim.purpose: Converts the scene into a blackmail bluff.
verbatim.text: “Quit fooling! How much do you know? And how much do you want?”
“You see,” explained Tuppence still sweetly, “I’m so very fond of money!”

voice_profile: Brisk, light omniscient narration that mostly yields to dialogue. Comedy comes from post-war slang ('old bean', 'stony', 'rag'), mock-formal narratorial labels ('Mr. Beresford magnificently', 'Miss Cowley told him'), and running jokes with setup and payoff. Tuppence is impulsive, mercenary in speech and quick at bluffing. Tommy is slow, dry and deflating. Exposition is kept spare. Suspense is planted through small, casual details: a name overheard, a clerk's name, a telephone message. Chapters often end on a cliffhanger line of dialogue. The prologue uses a graver register: plain, urgent, with short exchanges.
